name: paul-trap
description: A three-dimensional quadrupole ion trap: a driven ring with a grounded endcap either side of it, held on the axis of rotation. Axisymmetric, so it is a half-plane solve in (axial, radial) rather than a volume - which is the whole reason a 3-D trap is affordable here at all, and is SYM-1 doing exactly what it is for. The classical geometry has r0 squared equal to twice z0 squared, and with it the stability parameter q_z = 8 z e V / (m omega^2 (r0^2 + 2 z0^2)) collapses to 4 z e V / (m omega^2 r0^2) - the same volts per unit q as a linear quadrupole of the same inscribed radius, which makes the two directly comparable. The tabulated ejection boundary on the a = 0 line is q_z = 0.908. Expect this geometry to sit inside it: the electrodes here are flat annuli rather than hyperboloids, and a truncated flat approximation carries higher multipoles a hyperbola does not, the same way round rods do in a linear quadrupole. Measure it with the 'confined' figure of merit rather than a transmission - a trapped ion never arrives anywhere, so an arrival count cannot tell a working trap from one that lost everything.

inscribedRadius.description: r0, the radius of the ring's inner surface. Every Mathieu parameter here is quoted against it.

endcapHalfSpacing.description: z0, half the distance between the endcaps. Derived, because the classical trap has r0^2 = 2 z0^2 and departing from that is a different device rather than a different size. Change inscribedRadius and the whole trap scales.

rfAmplitude.description: Drive amplitude on the ring, zero to peak. The endcaps are grounded, which is the usual arrangement and is what makes the trap one basis solve.

electrodeGap.description: Clearance between the ring and each endcap. A real trap needs one for the same reason: they are at different potentials and must not touch.

ringThickness.description: How far the ring extends radially beyond r0.

launchOffset.description: How far off centre the ion starts, applied along the axis and across it at once. Both are needed and for different reasons: an ion at the exact centre feels no field at all, and an ion offset only radially sits at the axial null forever, so the axial instability - which is the one that ejects first, since q_r is half q_z - would never be excited and the trap would look stable at any amplitude.

cellsPerRadius.description: Mesh density, in cells across the inscribed radius. The knob a convergence study turns.

cycles.description: How many RF cycles to hold for. Not a convenience: the growth rate goes to zero at the stability edge, so a marginally unstable ion needs a long time to reach an electrode and a window shorter than that reports the window rather than the design. Measured on this geometry - at 60 cycles the ejection boundary is a ragged strip of survivors from 674 to 690 V, and at 200 it is a clean step between 672 and 674.

ringHalfLength.description: The ring stops short of the endcaps by the gap, so the two never occupy the same space - which the validator now refuses outright.

endcapOuterRadius.description: The endcaps stop short of the ring radially, again by the gap.

domainHalfLength.description: Half the axial extent of the solve, with room beyond the endcaps for the field to decay.

holdTime.description: Derived from the cycle count, so changing the drive frequency does not silently change how long the trap is held.

escapeDistance.description: Where the detector sits: outside the trap, so reaching it means having escaped. That is what makes the three outcomes distinct - struck an electrode, escaped, or still held.
